original.title: Fat-soluble vitamins
original.explanation: These four vitamins depend on intact intestinal lipid absorption for dietary uptake and can be deficient in fat malabsorption.

revised.title: Fat-soluble vitamins
revised.explanation: These are the standard chemical forms of vitamins A, D, E and K, which depend on intact intestinal fat absorption.

PLX-BCH-008.detail: Vitamins A, D, E and K are absorbed with dietary lipid in micelles and carried in chylomicrons, so they become deficient in fat malabsorption (cystic fibrosis, pancreatic insufficiency, celiac disease, cholestasis). They are stored in tissue and can accumulate to toxic levels, unlike most water-soluble vitamins. Vitamin D can also be made in skin and vitamin K by gut bacteria, but dietary uptake of both still requires fat absorption.
tileNotes: Retinol is vitamin A, needed for rhodopsin in rod photoreceptors and for epithelial differentiation.
Cholecalciferol is vitamin D3, made in skin with UV light or absorbed from the diet, then hydroxylated in liver and kidney.
Tocopherol is vitamin E, a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects membranes from peroxidation.
Phylloquinone is vitamin K1, the plant form of vitamin K required for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors.
PLX-BCH-008.changeSummary: Vitamin letter names replaced with their standard chemical names (retinol, cholecalciferol, tocopherol, phylloquinone).
PLX-BCH-008.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Introduction to Vitamins, PDF p. 127; Lipid Metabolism > Lipid Digestion and Absorption, PDF p. 83

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Chemical names remove the letter giveaway; cholecalciferol and phylloquinone are the standard D3 and K1 forms and all four remain fat-soluble vitamins.

original.title: Enzymes requiring copper
original.explanation: Copper is a required cofactor for each, linking it to oxidative phosphorylation, pigment formation, connective-tissue cross-linking, and cytosolic antioxidant defense.

revised.title: Enzymes requiring copper
revised.explanation: Copper is a required cofactor for each enzyme, linking it to oxidative phosphorylation, pigment formation, collagen cross-linking and cytosolic antioxidant defense.

PLX-BCH-011.detail: Copper deficiency, as in Menkes disease, impairs all of these enzymes, which explains its combination of neurologic decline, hypopigmentation, connective tissue fragility and oxidative injury. Superoxide dismutase 1 is the cytosolic copper-zinc isoform; mitochondrial superoxide dismutase 2 uses manganese instead and would not fit. Zinc-dependent enzymes such as carbonic anhydrase are a common look-alike group.
tileNotes: Cytochrome c oxidase is complex IV of the electron transport chain. Its copper centers transfer electrons to oxygen.
Tyrosinase converts tyrosine toward melanin. Copper is its catalytic metal, so copper deficiency causes hypopigmentation.
Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen and elastin. It is copper-dependent, and its loss in Menkes disease weakens connective tissue and vessels.
Superoxide dismutase 1 is the cytosolic copper-zinc enzyme that converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. Copper is its catalytic metal.
PLX-BCH-011.changeSummary: Tile 4 renamed from 'Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD1)' to 'Superoxide dismutase 1', the same enzyme without the copper symbol.
PLX-BCH-011.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Trace Elements, PDF p. 140; Connective Tissue > Menkes Disease, PDF p. 28

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Removing the copper symbol from tile 4 removes a real giveaway; SOD1 is correctly the cytosolic Cu/Zn isoform.

original.title: Findings associated with primary ciliary dyskinesia
original.explanation: Dysfunctional motile cilia impair airway clearance and sperm motility; abnormal embryonic nodal cilia can disrupt organ laterality.

revised.title: Findings associated with primary ciliary dyskinesia
revised.explanation: Defective motile cilia impair mucociliary clearance in the airways, sinuses and middle ear and impair sperm motility.

PLX-BCH-022.detail: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is usually autosomal recessive and often involves dynein arm defects. Poor clearance causes chronic wet cough, bronchiectasis, chronic rhinosinusitis and recurrent or chronic otitis media from childhood, and immotile sperm cause male infertility. Cystic fibrosis shares bronchiectasis, sinusitis and male infertility, but CF infertility comes from absent vas deferens rather than immotile sperm, and chronic otitis media is far more typical of PCD. Situs inversus occurs in about half of patients (Kartagener syndrome).
tileNotes: Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation from repeated infection when cilia cannot clear mucus.
Recurrent sinusitis reflects failed ciliary clearance of the paranasal sinuses and is nearly universal in PCD.
Chronic otitis media results from poor ciliary clearance of the middle ear and eustachian tube and is a typical childhood feature of PCD.
Male infertility occurs because sperm flagella share the defective axoneme and are immotile.
PLX-BCH-022.changeSummary: Tile 3 'Situs inversus' replaced with 'Chronic otitis media'.
PLX-BCH-022.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Cell Biology > Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, PDF p. 9

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Chronic otitis media is a standard PCD feature and the CF contrast in the detail is correct.

original.title: Characteristic clues for Tay-Sachs disease
original.explanation: Deficient hexosaminidase A allows GM2 storage, producing characteristic retinal and lysosomal findings.

revised.title: Characteristic clues for Tay-Sachs disease
revised.explanation: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes neuronal GM2 storage, producing hyperacusis, a cherry-red macula and lamellated lysosomes.

PLX-BCH-024.detail: Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease, more common in Ashkenazi Jewish populations, with progressive neurodegeneration beginning in infancy. An exaggerated startle to sound is an early sign. Niemann-Pick disease also has a cherry-red macula but has hepatosplenomegaly and foamy macrophages, while Tay-Sachs has no hepatosplenomegaly.
tileNotes: An exaggerated startle response (hyperacusis) to noise is a classic early neurologic sign in infants with Tay-Sachs disease.
GM2 ganglioside accumulates because hexosaminidase A cannot degrade it, mainly in neurons.
A cherry-red macula appears because lipid-laden retinal ganglion cells surround the fovea, which lacks them.
Onion-skin lysosomes are concentric lamellated lysosomal inclusions of stored ganglioside seen on electron microscopy.
PLX-BCH-024.changeSummary: Tile 1 'Hexosaminidase A deficiency' replaced with 'Exaggerated startle response'.
PLX-BCH-024.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Tay-Sachs Disease, PDF p. 14

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Hyperacusis/exaggerated startle is a classic Tay-Sachs sign and removing the enzyme name requires more reasoning.

original.title: Characteristic Gaucher disease findings
original.explanation: Glucocerebroside storage in macrophages and involvement of bone, liver, and spleen explain these associations.

revised.title: Characteristic Gaucher disease findings
revised.explanation: Glucocerebroside-laden macrophages infiltrate the marrow, bone, liver and spleen, producing cytopenias, bone disease and organomegaly.

PLX-BCH-026.detail: Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucocerebrosidase and the most common lysosomal storage disease. Storage macrophages (Gaucher cells) cause hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia from hypersplenism and marrow infiltration, bone pain crises, avascular necrosis of the femoral head and osteopenia. Sickle cell disease can also cause bone crises and avascular necrosis, but it causes hemolytic anemia and autosplenectomy rather than splenomegaly with pancytopenia in adults.
tileNotes: Pancytopenia results from hypersplenism and replacement of the marrow by Gaucher cells.
Bone crises are episodes of severe bone pain caused by marrow infiltration and bone infarction.
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is a classic skeletal complication of Gaucher disease.
Hepatosplenomegaly reflects accumulation of glucocerebroside-laden macrophages in the liver and spleen.
PLX-BCH-026.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Gaucher Disease, PDF p. 18

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Pancytopenia is a standard Gaucher finding; removing the pathognomonic histology tile adds difficulty.

original.title: Diagnostic associations of metachromatic leukodystrophy
original.explanation: Deficient arylsulfatase A prevents sulfatide breakdown; storage causes demyelination and metachromatic staining of macrophage vacuoles.

revised.title: Diagnostic associations of metachromatic leukodystrophy
revised.explanation: Arylsulfatase A deficiency prevents sulfatide breakdown, and sulfatide storage demyelinates the central and peripheral nervous systems, causing ataxia.

PLX-BCH-028.detail: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease. Sulfatide accumulates in myelin-forming cells, causing demyelination in both the brain and peripheral nerves, which presents with ataxia, gait disturbance and later dementia. Krabbe disease also demyelinates both systems but is caused by galactocerebrosidase deficiency with globoid cells, and adrenoleukodystrophy is a peroxisomal disorder with very long chain fatty acid accumulation.
tileNotes: Arylsulfatase A is the lysosomal enzyme deficient in metachromatic leukodystrophy.
Sulfatide (cerebroside sulfate) accumulates because arylsulfatase A cannot remove its sulfate group.
Sulfatide storage damages oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, so demyelination involves both central and peripheral nerves.
Ataxia and gait disturbance are typical presenting features in late-infantile and juvenile metachromatic leukodystrophy.
PLX-BCH-028.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Lysosomal Storage Diseases > Metachromatic Leukodystrophy, PDF p. 16

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Ataxia is a standard MLD presentation and removes the 'metachromatic' giveaway.

original.title: Classical Ehlers-Danlos findings
original.explanation: Classical EDS combines joint and skin extensibility with tissue fragility, abnormal scarring, and poor healing.

revised.title: Classical Ehlers-Danlos findings
revised.explanation: Defective collagen in classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome makes skin and vessels fragile and stretchy and impairs healing.

PLX-BCH-029.detail: Classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is usually caused by type V collagen mutations (COL5A1, COL5A2). It combines skin hyperextensibility, widened atrophic scars, easy bruising and poor wound healing with joint hypermobility. Scurvy and bleeding disorders also cause easy bruising and poor healing, but they do not cause hyperextensible skin or atrophic scars.
tileNotes: Easy bruising reflects fragile capillaries and perivascular connective tissue in classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Hyperextensible skin stretches beyond normal and recoils, a major feature of classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Atrophic scars are wide, thin scars that form because collagen in healing skin is defective.
Poor wound healing results from abnormal collagen fibril formation, so wounds split and heal slowly.
PLX-BCH-029.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Connective Tissue > Ehlers Danlos Syndrome, PDF p. 27

review.note: Easy bruising is a standard classical EDS feature; COL5A1/COL5A2 attribution is correct.

original.title: Characteristic Menkes disease clues
original.explanation: Impaired copper export from enterocytes (ATP7A) causes systemic copper deficiency, with characteristic hair and pigmentation changes and low circulating copper and ceruloplasmin.

revised.title: Characteristic Menkes disease clues
revised.explanation: Defective ATP7A copper export causes systemic copper deficiency, producing infantile hypotonia, hypopigmentation and low serum copper and ceruloplasmin.

PLX-BCH-030.detail: Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive disorder of ATP7A, so copper absorbed by enterocytes cannot reach the circulation. Copper-dependent enzymes fail, causing hypotonia, seizures, developmental regression, hypopigmentation, kinky hair and vascular fragility in male infants. Wilson disease (ATP7B) also has low ceruloplasmin, but it presents later with copper overload in the liver and brain.
tileNotes: Hypotonia is a characteristic neurologic finding in infants with Menkes disease, from copper-deficient neurodegeneration.
Hypopigmentation of skin and hair results from reduced activity of tyrosinase, a copper-dependent enzyme.
Serum copper is low because ATP7A defects block copper export from enterocytes into the blood.
Ceruloplasmin is low because little copper reaches the liver to be incorporated into it.
PLX-BCH-030.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Connective Tissue > Menkes Disease, PDF p. 28

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Hypotonia is a characteristic Menkes finding and removing kinky hair removes the giveaway.

original.title: B vitamins supplying PDH and alpha-KGDH cofactors
original.explanation: These vitamins supply TPP, FAD, NAD+, and CoA for both the pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes; lipoic acid is the additional nonvitamin cofactor.

revised.title: B vitamins supplying PDH and alpha-KGDH cofactors
revised.explanation: These vitamins supply TPP, FAD, NAD+ and CoA for both the pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes.

PLX-BCH-032.detail: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase share the same five cofactors: thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD+. Four come from B vitamins (B1, B5, B2 and B3); lipoic acid is the fifth, nonvitamin cofactor. Pyridoxine (B6) and biotin (B7) are not used by these complexes; biotin is the cofactor for carboxylases such as pyruvate carboxylase.
tileNotes: Thiamine (B1) becomes thiamine pyrophosphate, which decarboxylates the alpha-keto acid substrate.
Riboflavin (B2) becomes FAD, which reoxidizes the lipoamide arm in the dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase step.
Niacin (B3) becomes NAD+, the final electron acceptor that leaves the complex as NADH.
Pantothenic acid (B5) is part of coenzyme A, which accepts the acyl group to form acetyl-CoA or succinyl-CoA.
PLX-BCH-032.changeSummary: Vitamin B number names replaced with thiamine, riboflavin, niacin and pantothenic acid.
PLX-BCH-032.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Energy Production > Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex and TCA Cycle, PDF pp. 36-37

original.title: Hormones that increase PEPCK in the source
original.explanation: These four hormones increase PEP carboxykinase per the source, supporting increased glucose production.

revised.title: Hormones that induce PEPCK expression
revised.explanation: Each hormone increases transcription of the gene for PEP carboxykinase, a key regulated step of gluconeogenesis.

PLX-BCH-034.detail: PEP carboxykinase converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate and is regulated mainly by changes in gene expression. Glucagon and epinephrine raise cAMP and activate CREB, cortisol acts through the glucocorticoid receptor, and thyroid hormone acts through its nuclear receptor; all increase PEPCK transcription. Insulin represses PEPCK transcription. Growth hormone is a counterregulatory hormone but is not a classic PEPCK inducer, so this group is narrower than counterregulatory hormones.
tileNotes: Glucagon raises hepatic cAMP, which activates CREB and increases PEPCK transcription during fasting.
Cortisol binds the glucocorticoid receptor, which acts on glucocorticoid response elements of the PEPCK gene.
Epinephrine also raises hepatic cAMP, inducing PEPCK by the same CREB pathway as glucagon.
Thyroid hormone (T3) acts through its nuclear receptor to increase PEPCK gene transcription.
PLX-BCH-034.changeSummary: Title changed from 'Hormones that increase PEPCK in the source' to 'Hormones that induce PEPCK expression'; tiles unchanged.
PLX-BCH-034.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Carbohydrates > Gluconeogenesis, PDF p. 43

original.title: Diagnostic clues for maple syrup urine disease
original.explanation: Deficient branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase causes accumulation of BCAAs and their ketoacids, with characteristic urine odor and neurologic dysfunction.

revised.title: Features of maple syrup urine disease
revised.explanation: Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causes accumulation of leucine, isoleucine and valine, with a sweet urine odor and neurotoxicity.

PLX-BCH-051.detail: Maple syrup urine disease is an autosomal recessive defect of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. Newborns present with poor feeding, vomiting, encephalopathy and abnormal tone or dystonia, and the urine and cerumen smell like maple syrup. Leucine is the most neurotoxic metabolite, and acute decompensation can cause life-threatening cerebral edema. Treatment restricts branched-chain amino acids, and some patients respond to thiamine.
tileNotes: Sweet-smelling urine comes from accumulated branched-chain ketoacids and their derivatives, giving the maple syrup odor.
Plasma leucine, isoleucine and valine are elevated because their ketoacids cannot be oxidatively decarboxylated.
Cerebral edema is a dangerous complication of acute metabolic decompensation, driven mainly by high leucine.
Dystonia and other abnormal tone are neurologic manifestations of branched-chain amino acid toxicity in affected infants.
PLX-BCH-051.changeSummary: Tile 3 'Elevated branched-chain ketoacids' replaced with 'Cerebral edema', and the title tightened from 'Diagnostic clues for' to 'Features of' maple syrup urine disease, since cerebral edema is a complication rather than a diagnostic clue.
PLX-BCH-051.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Protein Metabolism > Branched Chain Amino Acids, PDF p. 110

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Cerebral edema is a recognized life-threatening MSUD complication and the title change to 'Features' fits it.

original.title: Source-described sideroblastic anemia findings
original.explanation: Defective heme production traps iron in erythroid mitochondria, producing this marrow, blood-film, red-cell-size, and iron pattern.

revised.title: Classic sideroblastic anemia findings
revised.explanation: Defective heme synthesis traps iron in erythroblast mitochondria, producing ringed sideroblasts, stippled microcytic red cells and iron overload labs.

PLX-BCH-054.detail: Sideroblastic anemia results from impaired protoporphyrin synthesis, as with X-linked ALA synthase defects, alcohol, lead, isoniazid or vitamin B6 deficiency. Iron enters the mitochondria but cannot be incorporated into heme, so it accumulates around the nucleus as ringed sideroblasts, while red cells are microcytic and serum iron and ferritin rise. Iron deficiency is also microcytic but has low serum iron, and lead poisoning shares basophilic stippling.
tileNotes: Ringed sideroblasts are erythroid precursors with iron-laden mitochondria surrounding the nucleus, seen with Prussian blue stain of marrow.
Basophilic stippling is coarse blue granules of residual ribosomal RNA in red cells, seen in sideroblastic anemia and lead poisoning.
Microcytosis occurs because hemoglobin production is reduced when heme cannot be made.
Serum iron is elevated because iron is absorbed and delivered but not used for heme synthesis.
PLX-BCH-054.changeSummary: Removed the 'Source-described' prefix from the title; tiles unchanged.
PLX-BCH-054.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Porphyrias > Heme Synthesis Regulation and Sideroblastic Anemia, PDF p. 121; Vitamins > Vitamin B6, PDF p. 136

original.title: Source-listed precipitants of AIP attacks
original.explanation: These exposures can precipitate attacks in susceptible individuals by inducing ALAS1/CYP demand in the setting of impaired heme precursor processing.

revised.title: Precipitants of acute intermittent porphyria attacks
revised.explanation: Each exposure induces hepatic ALA synthase, increasing porphyrin precursor production when porphobilinogen deaminase is deficient.

PLX-BCH-055.detail: Acute intermittent porphyria is an autosomal dominant deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase. Anything that raises hepatic heme demand, especially CYP450-inducing drugs, derepresses ALA synthase, so ALA and porphobilinogen accumulate and cause abdominal pain, neuropathy and psychiatric symptoms. Other classic triggers include sulfonamides, fasting and progesterone. Treatment is glucose and hemin, which suppress ALA synthase.
tileNotes: Barbiturates induce CYP450 enzymes, raising heme demand and ALA synthase activity.
Phenytoin is an enzyme-inducing antiseizure drug that can precipitate attacks.
Alcohol induces hepatic ALA synthase and CYP450 enzymes and is a recognized trigger.
Smoking induces hepatic CYP enzymes and is a recognized trigger of acute attacks.
PLX-BCH-055.changeSummary: Removed the 'Source-listed' prefix and spelled out acute intermittent porphyria in the title; tiles unchanged.
PLX-BCH-055.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Porphyrias > Acute Intermittent Porphyria, PDF p. 122

original.title: Ocular findings of vitamin A deficiency
original.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency impairs rod vision and causes ocular surface injury, producing these classic findings.

revised.title: Findings of vitamin A deficiency
revised.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency impairs rod function and epithelial differentiation, affecting the eye and the skin.

PLX-BCH-057.detail: Retinal is required for rhodopsin, so the earliest symptom is night blindness. Retinoic acid maintains specialized epithelium, and its loss causes keratinizing metaplasia: conjunctival Bitot spots, corneal softening and ulceration (keratomalacia) and follicular hyperkeratosis of the skin. Deficiency also increases infection risk, especially measles severity. Vitamin A toxicity, by contrast, causes headache, intracranial hypertension and teratogenicity.
tileNotes: Night blindness occurs because rods need retinal to regenerate rhodopsin.
Bitot spots are foamy, keratinized plaques on the bulbar conjunctiva from squamous metaplasia.
Follicular hyperkeratosis is keratin plugging of hair follicles on the skin, a classic cutaneous sign of vitamin A deficiency.
Keratomalacia is softening and ulceration of the cornea in severe deficiency, which can lead to blindness.
PLX-BCH-057.changeSummary: Replaced 'Xerophthalmia' with 'Follicular hyperkeratosis' and broadened the title from ocular findings to findings of vitamin A deficiency.
PLX-BCH-057.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamin A, PDF p. 128

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Follicular hyperkeratosis is a classic vitamin A deficiency skin sign and removes the xerophthalmia umbrella-term overlap.

original.title: Classic skeletal findings of rickets
original.explanation: Deficient mineralization of growing bone produces these limb, costochondral, and skull findings.

revised.title: Classic skeletal findings of rickets
revised.explanation: Deficient mineralization of growing bone and growth plates produces these limb, rib and skull findings.

PLX-BCH-059.detail: Rickets is defective mineralization of the growth plate and osteoid in children, most often from vitamin D deficiency but also from phosphate wasting and other causes. Soft bone bends under weight (genu varum), unmineralized cartilage expands at the costochondral junctions, and the skull is soft with slow fontanelle closure. Adults with the same mineralization defect have osteomalacia, without growth plate or skull findings.
tileNotes: Bowed legs (genu varum) develop when undermineralized long bones bend under body weight.
Costochondral beading (the rachitic rosary) is palpable enlargement of the rib costochondral junctions from excess unmineralized cartilage.
Craniotabes is softening of the skull bones that yields to pressure, an early sign in infants.
Delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle reflects slow mineralization of the skull.
PLX-BCH-059.changeSummary: Tile 2 'Rachitic rosary' renamed 'Costochondral beading', the same finding without the rickets root.
PLX-BCH-059.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamin D, PDF p. 129

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Costochondral beading is the same finding as rachitic rosary without the rickets root, a real giveaway removal.

original.title: Syndromes associated with thiamine deficiency
original.explanation: Thiamine deficiency causes acute and chronic neurocognitive syndromes and neurologic or cardiovascular beriberi.

revised.title: Manifestations of thiamine deficiency
revised.explanation: Thiamine deficiency impairs glucose oxidation in neurons and myocardium, causing encephalopathy, amnesia, neuropathy and high-output cardiac failure.

PLX-BCH-060.detail: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase. Deficiency, classically in alcohol use disorder or malnutrition, causes Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) and Korsakoff amnestic syndrome. Dry beriberi is a symmetric peripheral neuropathy, and wet beriberi is high-output heart failure from peripheral vasodilation. Giving glucose before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
tileNotes: Wernicke encephalopathy is acute confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia with damage to the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray.
Korsakoff syndrome is chronic anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation following Wernicke encephalopathy.
Symmetric peripheral neuropathy with distal sensory and motor loss is dry beriberi.
High-output heart failure from peripheral vasodilation, with edema, is wet beriberi.
PLX-BCH-060.changeSummary: Dry and wet beriberi replaced by the findings they denote (symmetric peripheral neuropathy and high-output heart failure), and the title changed from syndromes to manifestations.
PLX-BCH-060.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamin B1, PDF p. 133

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Replacing dry and wet beriberi with the findings they denote requires more reasoning and is accurate.

original.title: Contributors to niacin deficiency
original.explanation: Inadequate intake, impaired tryptophan-to-niacin conversion (B6), reduced tryptophan absorption (Hartnup), and diversion of tryptophan to serotonin (carcinoid) each reduce niacin availability.

revised.title: Contributors to niacin deficiency
revised.explanation: Each reduces niacin supply, through poor dietary niacin, impaired tryptophan-to-niacin conversion, reduced tryptophan absorption or diversion of tryptophan to serotonin.

PLX-BCH-061.detail: Niacin comes from the diet and from tryptophan, a pathway that requires vitamin B6. Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia) results when either source fails. Corn contains niacin in a poorly available bound form and is low in tryptophan; Hartnup disease impairs neutral amino acid absorption; carcinoid tumors consume tryptophan to make serotonin. Isoniazid causes deficiency by depleting B6.
tileNotes: A corn-based diet is the classic dietary cause of pellagra because corn niacin is bound and corn is low in tryptophan.
Vitamin B6 is needed to convert tryptophan to niacin, so B6 deficiency reduces endogenous niacin synthesis.
Hartnup disease is a defect in neutral amino acid transport that reduces intestinal and renal tryptophan uptake.
Carcinoid syndrome diverts tryptophan to serotonin synthesis, leaving less for niacin.
PLX-BCH-061.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamin B3, PDF p. 135; Protein Metabolism > Tryptophan, Niacin, and Serotonin, PDF p. 107

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Corn-based diet is the classic dietary cause of pellagra and the explanation is correct.

original.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency diagnostic associations
original.explanation: B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and both homocysteine and methylmalonyl-CoA metabolism, and causes characteristic spinal cord injury.

revised.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency diagnostic associations
revised.explanation: B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and homocysteine remethylation and damages myelin in the spinal cord.

PLX-BCH-063.detail: B12 is needed by methionine synthase (homocysteine to methionine, regenerating tetrahydrofolate) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Impaired DNA synthesis causes megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, and homocysteine rises. Folate deficiency shares the anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils and high homocysteine, but it does not raise methylmalonic acid or cause subacute combined degeneration.
tileNotes: Megaloblastic anemia results from impaired DNA synthesis with nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony in marrow precursors.
Homocysteine rises because methionine synthase needs B12 to remethylate it.
Hypersegmented neutrophils, with six or more lobes, are a peripheral smear sign of megaloblastic anemia.
Subacute combined degeneration is demyelination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, specific to B12 rather than folate deficiency.
PLX-BCH-063.changeSummary: Tile 3 'Elevated methylmalonic acid' replaced with 'Hypersegmented neutrophils'.
PLX-BCH-063.source: Bootcamp.com Biochemistry Jan 2025(1).pdf; Vitamins > Vitamins B9 and B12, PDF p. 138

review.reviewer: Claude (AI), two independent passes: finalize, then a separate check
review.note: Hypersegmented neutrophils are a standard B12 deficiency finding; subacute combined degeneration still anchors B12 over folate.

original.title: Zinc-dependent enzymes
original.explanation: Zinc is a cofactor for each enzyme or family, linking it to peptide processing, acid-base chemistry, phosphate hydrolysis, and DNA synthesis.

revised.title: Zinc-dependent enzymes
revised.explanation: Each is a zinc metalloenzyme that requires zinc at its active site for catalysis.

PLX-BCH-064.detail: Zinc is a catalytic or structural cofactor for many enzymes and forms zinc finger motifs in transcription factors. These four are standard examples spanning peptide cleavage, carbon dioxide hydration, phosphate ester hydrolysis and ethanol oxidation. Zinc deficiency causes delayed wound healing, hypogonadism, dysgeusia, alopecia and acrodermatitis. Copper-dependent enzymes such as lysyl oxidase and tyrosinase are the main look-alike group.

original.explanation: Marked glomerular protein loss lowers serum albumin and promotes edema; altered lipid metabolism produces hyperlipidemia. Adult nephrotic-range proteinuria is typically above 3.5 g/day.

The parasympathetic fibers run superficially on the nerve, so compressive lesions such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm affect them early, producing a dilated pupil and loss of accommodation. Ischemic (diabetic) palsies damage the core of the nerve and classically spare the pupil. The unopposed lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) leave the eye resting down and out.

The medial, superior and inferior recti and inferior oblique are paralyzed, so adduction, elevation and depression are impaired. Abduction (CN VI) and intorsion (CN IV) are preserved.

original.title: Retrochiasmal sites causing homonymous visual field loss
original.explanation: Unilateral lesions posterior to the optic chiasm disrupt corresponding portions of the contralateral visual field in both eyes (homonymous defects).

revised.title: Retrochiasmal sites causing homonymous visual field loss
revised.explanation: A unilateral lesion at any of these sites, all posterior to the optic chiasm, causes a homonymous defect in the contralateral visual field of both eyes.

NEU-023.detail: Behind the chiasm, each side of the visual pathway carries fibers from the ipsilateral temporal retina and contralateral nasal retina, representing the contralateral visual hemifield. Lesions anywhere from the optic tract to the occipital cortex therefore produce homonymous defects. Optic nerve lesions cause monocular loss and chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia, so neither is homonymous.

Meyer loop is the inferior part of the optic radiation that sweeps through the temporal lobe, carrying fibers from the inferior retina. A lesion causes a contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

The primary visual cortex lies along the calcarine fissure of the occipital lobe. A lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing in posterior cerebral artery infarction.

original.title: Causes of conductive hearing loss
original.explanation: These conditions impair external- or middle-ear sound transmission rather than primarily damaging cochlear sensory transduction.

revised.title: Causes of conductive hearing loss
revised.explanation: Each impairs transmission of sound through the external or middle ear rather than damaging the cochlea or auditory nerve.

NEU-024.detail: Conductive hearing loss arises when sound cannot reach the inner ear efficiently. On tuning fork testing, bone conduction exceeds air conduction on the affected side (Rinne negative) and the Weber test lateralizes to the affected ear. Sensorineural loss, from cochlear or CN VIII damage (presbycusis, noise, acoustic neuroma), gives Rinne positive with Weber lateralizing to the normal ear.
tileNotes: Impacted cerumen occludes the external auditory canal and blocks sound from reaching the tympanic membrane.
Middle ear effusion or pus in otitis media damps movement of the tympanic membrane and ossicles.
Otosclerosis is abnormal bone remodeling that fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, typically causing progressive conductive loss in young adults.
A perforated tympanic membrane loses surface area and vibratory efficiency, reducing sound transfer to the ossicles.

original.title: Peripheral causes of vertigo
original.explanation: These disorders affect the peripheral vestibular apparatus or CN VIII and can produce vertigo with differing timing and hearing features.

revised.title: Peripheral causes of vertigo
revised.explanation: Each disorder affects the inner ear vestibular apparatus or the vestibular nerve, producing true rotational vertigo of peripheral origin.

NEU-026.detail: Peripheral vertigo arises from the labyrinth or vestibular nerve and is usually accompanied by horizontal or torsional nystagmus that is suppressed by visual fixation, without other brainstem signs. The disorders differ by timing and hearing: BPPV causes brief positional episodes, vestibular neuritis causes days of continuous vertigo with normal hearing, labyrinthitis adds hearing loss, and Meniere disease causes recurrent attacks lasting hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. Central vertigo (cerebellar or brainstem stroke, MS) is the key contrast and may cause vertical or direction-changing nystagmus and other neurologic deficits.

Vestibular neuritis is inflammation of the vestibular nerve, usually presumed viral, causing acute continuous vertigo lasting days with preserved hearing.
Meniere disease is endolymphatic hydrops causing recurrent vertigo attacks with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
Labyrinthitis is inflammation of the inner ear labyrinth, causing acute vertigo together with sensorineural hearing loss.

original.title: Posterior-canal BPPV associations
original.explanation: Displaced otoconia (canaliths) cause brief positional vertigo; posterior-canal BPPV is diagnosed with the Dix-Hallpike maneuver and treated with the Epley canalith-repositioning maneuver.

revised.title: Posterior-canal BPPV associations
revised.explanation: Free-floating otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal cause BPPV, which produces torsional upbeating nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike testing and is treated with the Epley repositioning maneuver.

NEU-027.detail: In posterior-canal BPPV, otoconia detached from the utricle move within the canal when the head changes position, deflecting the cupula. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver provokes, after a short latency, a fatigable burst of upbeating nystagmus with a torsional component toward the lower ear. The Epley maneuver moves the debris back into the utricle. Horizontal-canal BPPV instead produces horizontal nystagmus on the supine roll test and is treated with different maneuvers.

Posterior canal stimulation drives the eyes in that canal's plane, producing upbeating nystagmus with a torsional component toward the lower ear. It is brief, appears after a few seconds' latency, and fatigues with repetition.
The Dix-Hallpike maneuver moves the patient from sitting to supine with the head turned and extended, provoking vertigo and nystagmus from the dependent posterior canal.
The Epley maneuver is a sequence of head positions that moves the otoconia out of the posterior canal into the utricle, treating the vertigo.

original.title: Pilocytic astrocytoma associations
original.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a low-grade (WHO grade 1) astrocytic tumor, often cystic and cerebellar in children, with GFAP expression and characteristic Rosenthal fibers.

revised.title: Pilocytic astrocytoma associations
revised.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a low-grade (WHO grade 1) astrocytic tumor, often a cystic cerebellar mass in children, composed of GFAP-positive bipolar astrocytes with hair-like processes and containing Rosenthal fibers.

NEU-029.detail: Pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common primary brain tumor of childhood and has an excellent prognosis after resection. It classically appears as a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule in the cerebellum, though optic pathway and brainstem sites occur, especially with neurofibromatosis type 1. Histology shows elongated bipolar astrocytes with long, thin processes, eosinophilic Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies. Its well-circumscribed, low-grade behavior contrasts with diffuse astrocytomas and medulloblastoma, the other common posterior fossa tumor of childhood.
tileNotes: Rosenthal fibers are thick, eosinophilic, corkscrew-shaped intracytoplasmic inclusions of glial filaments. They are a characteristic histologic feature of pilocytic astrocytoma.
Glial fibrillary acidic protein is an intermediate filament of astrocytes, so this astrocytic tumor stains positive.
The tumor classically presents as a cerebellar cyst with a mural nodule in a child, causing ataxia or obstructive hydrocephalus.
The tumor cells are bipolar astrocytes with long, thin, hair-like processes, which give the tumor its name ('pilocytic' means hair cell).

original.title: Immunodeficiency-associated primary CNS lymphoma clues
original.explanation: Primary CNS lymphoma is usually a CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma (commonly DLBCL); its immunodeficiency-associated form is strongly linked to EBV.

revised.title: Immunodeficiency-associated primary CNS lymphoma clues
revised.explanation: Primary CNS lymphoma in an immunodeficient host is typically an EBV-driven, CD20-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that presents as an enhancing mass in the deep periventricular brain.

NEU-033.detail: Primary CNS lymphoma is an extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma confined to the brain, eyes, leptomeninges or spinal cord. On imaging it favors deep periventricular white matter and the corpus callosum, and in AIDS lesions are often multiple and ring-enhancing, so the main differential is toxoplasmosis. Nearly all cases are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas expressing CD20. EBV is present in almost all immunodeficiency-associated cases (for example AIDS with a low CD4 count), whereas immunocompetent cases are usually EBV-negative.
tileNotes: Primary CNS lymphoma classically forms enhancing lesions in the deep periventricular white matter and corpus callosum. In immunodeficient patients the enhancement is often ring-like, mimicking toxoplasmosis.
The large majority of primary CNS lymphomas are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas.
The tumor cells are mature B cells that express the pan-B-cell marker CD20.
In immunodeficiency, EBV-infected B cells escape T-cell control and drive lymphoma; EBV DNA in CSF supports the diagnosis in AIDS.

original.title: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome findings
original.explanation: Lateral medullary injury (PICA/vertebral) affects the nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract, spinothalamic tract, and descending sympathetic fibers.

revised.title: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome findings
revised.explanation: A lateral medullary infarct (PICA or vertebral artery) damages the nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, lateral spinothalamic tract and descending sympathetic fibers.

NEU-036.detail: Wallenberg syndrome produces a crossed sensory pattern: pain and temperature loss on the ipsilateral face (spinal trigeminal tract) and the contralateral body (spinothalamic tract, which has already crossed). Descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic fibers cause an ipsilateral Horner syndrome, and vestibular and cerebellar involvement add vertigo, nystagmus and ipsilateral ataxia. Involvement of the nucleus ambiguus (hoarseness, dysphagia, reduced gag) localizes the lesion to the medulla rather than the lateral pons, where facial nucleus involvement and hearing loss occur instead.
tileNotes: Damage to the nucleus ambiguus weakens the ipsilateral palatal, pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles (CN IX and X), causing hoarseness and dysphagia. This is the localizing sign for the medulla.
The spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract carry pain and temperature from the ipsilateral face, so their damage causes ipsilateral facial loss.
The lateral spinothalamic tract has already crossed in the spinal cord, so a lateral medullary lesion causes pain and temperature loss in the contralateral trunk and limbs.
Interruption of descending sympathetic fibers in the lateral medulla produces ipsilateral ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.

original.title: Epidural hematoma associations
original.explanation: A traumatic epidural hematoma classically involves middle meningeal arterial bleeding outside the dura with a biconvex CT collection that does not cross suture lines; some patients have a transient lucid interval.

revised.title: Epidural hematoma associations
revised.explanation: Epidural hematoma is classically arterial bleeding from a middle meningeal artery torn by a skull fracture at the pterion; the blood strips dura from the skull and is confined by the sutures, and some patients have a lucid interval.

NEU-038.detail: The pterion is the thin junction of the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones, and the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery runs beneath it. A fracture here tears the artery, and the blood collects between the skull and the periosteal dura. Because the dura is firmly attached at the sutures, the collection cannot spread past them and forms a biconvex shape on CT. A subdural hematoma, by contrast, results from torn bridging veins, lies beneath the dura, crosses suture lines and is crescent-shaped.
tileNotes: A temporal-region fracture at the pterion overlies and can tear the middle meningeal artery, the classic source of epidural bleeding.
The hematoma lies in the potential space between the inner table of the skull and the dura, which it strips away from the bone.
The dura is tightly adherent to the skull at the sutures, so an epidural collection is bounded by them, giving its biconvex (lentiform) shape on CT.
Some patients briefly lose consciousness, recover, then deteriorate as the arterial hematoma expands. It is a classic but inconsistent feature.

original.title: Subdural hematoma associations
original.explanation: Bridging-vein injury produces a crescentic subdural collection that can cross suture lines; cerebral atrophy (elderly, alcohol use) increases susceptibility.

revised.title: Subdural hematoma associations
revised.explanation: Subdural hematoma results from tearing of bridging veins, so blood collects beneath the dura, can spread across suture lines, and occurs more easily when cerebral atrophy stretches those veins.

NEU-039.detail: Bridging veins cross the subdural space from the cortex to the dural venous sinuses, and acceleration-deceleration forces can tear them. Because the collection lies beneath the dura, it is not limited by sutures and spreads over the hemisphere as a crescent on CT, though it does not cross the midline falx. Brain atrophy in older adults and people with chronic alcohol use stretches the veins and widens the subdural space, increasing risk; infants (abusive head trauma) and anticoagulated patients are also at risk. Epidural hematoma is the contrast: arterial, above the dura, and bounded by sutures.
tileNotes: Bridging veins run from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses and tear with acceleration-deceleration injury, the classic source of subdural bleeding.
The blood collects in the subdural space between the inner dural layer and the arachnoid.
Because the collection lies beneath the dura, the sutures do not limit it, and it spreads along the convexity as a crescent-shaped collection.
Cerebral atrophy stretches the bridging veins across a wider subdural space, so older adults can develop a subdural hematoma after minor trauma, often chronic.
NEU-039.changeSummary: Replaced 'Crescent-shaped (concave) CT collection' with 'Crosses suture lines'.

original.title: Subarachnoid hemorrhage clues
tiles: Blood in basal cisterns on CT
original.explanation: Blood in the subarachnoid space (often ruptured aneurysm) causes abrupt severe headache and meningeal irritation and may be seen in the basal cisterns on CT or detected as CSF xanthochromia.

revised.title: Subarachnoid hemorrhage associations
tiles: Blood in basal cisterns on CT
revised.explanation: Blood in the subarachnoid space, most often from a ruptured saccular aneurysm, irritates the meninges, appears in the basal cisterns on CT, is broken down to give CSF xanthochromia, and can trigger vasospasm days later.

NEU-040.detail: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage classically presents with a sudden severe headache. Noncontrast CT shows hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and sulci and is most sensitive early; if CT is negative, lumbar puncture after several hours can show xanthochromia from hemoglobin breakdown. Blood breakdown products around the cerebral arteries can cause vasospasm, typically between days 3 and 14, leading to delayed ischemic deficits; nimodipine is given to improve outcome. Rebleeding, hydrocephalus and hyponatremia are other complications.
tileNotes: Arterial narrowing provoked by blood breakdown products in the subarachnoid space typically occurs 3 to 14 days after the bleed and can cause delayed cerebral ischemia.
Subarachnoid blood irritates the meninges, producing neck stiffness, often developing hours after the bleed.
Acute subarachnoid blood is hyperdense on noncontrast CT and collects in the basal cisterns around the circle of Willis.
Red cells lysed in CSF release hemoglobin, which is converted to bilirubin over several hours, giving the CSF a yellow color. This helps distinguish true hemorrhage from a traumatic tap.

original.title: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome clues
original.explanation: A pineal-region or dorsal midbrain lesion disrupts pretectal eye-movement circuitry (posterior commissure, riMLF) and can obstruct the cerebral aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus.

revised.title: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome clues
revised.explanation: A dorsal midbrain lesion, classically a pineal region tumor, disrupts pretectal and posterior commissure eye-movement pathways and can compress the cerebral aqueduct, causing obstructive hydrocephalus.

NEU-047.detail: Parinaud syndrome results from damage to the dorsal midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus and posterior commissure, most often from a pineal germinoma in a young male, but also from hydrocephalus, midbrain stroke or MS. The core eye findings are impaired upgaze, pupils that react poorly to light but constrict with near effort, convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze and eyelid retraction (Collier sign). Compression of the aqueduct of Sylvius blocks CSF outflow from the third ventricle, causing noncommunicating hydrocephalus. Light-near dissociation also occurs with neurosyphilis (Argyll Robertson pupils) and vertical gaze palsy with progressive supranuclear palsy, which are look-alikes.
tileNotes: Damage to the vertical gaze centers and posterior commissure in the dorsal midbrain impairs upward gaze first.
The pretectal light reflex pathway is interrupted while the more ventral near-response pathway is spared, so the pupils constrict to accommodation but not to light.
On attempted upgaze, the eyes converge and retract into the orbits in jerky movements, a characteristic sign of dorsal midbrain dysfunction.
A pineal region mass compresses the cerebral aqueduct, blocking CSF flow and causing noncommunicating hydrocephalus, which can itself worsen the dorsal midbrain signs.

original.title: Major dopaminergic pathways
original.explanation: These four classic dopamine circuits underlie reward/positive psychotic symptoms, cortical/negative symptoms, movement, and prolactin inhibition respectively.

revised.title: Major dopaminergic pathways
revised.explanation: These are the four classic dopamine pathways, which mediate reward and positive psychotic symptoms, cognition and negative symptoms, motor control, and inhibition of prolactin release respectively.

NEU-049.detail: Dopamine pathways explain both the therapeutic and adverse effects of antipsychotics. D2 blockade in the mesolimbic pathway reduces positive symptoms, while reduced mesocortical activity is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms. Blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway causes extrapyramidal symptoms, and in the tuberoinfundibular pathway it removes dopamine's inhibition of prolactin, causing hyperprolactinemia with galactorrhea and amenorrhea.
tileNotes: The mesolimbic pathway projects from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens and limbic structures. Overactivity is associated with positive psychotic symptoms, and it is the main target of antipsychotics.
The mesocortical pathway projects from the ventral tegmental area to the prefrontal cortex. Reduced activity is associated with negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia.

The nigrostriatal pathway projects from the substantia nigra pars compacta to the striatum and controls movement. Its degeneration causes Parkinson disease and its blockade causes extrapyramidal symptoms.
The tuberoinfundibular pathway projects from the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus to the median eminence, where dopamine inhibits prolactin secretion. Blockade causes hyperprolactinemia.

original.title: Alzheimer disease neuropathology clues
original.explanation: Alzheimer pathology features extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles made of hyperphosphorylated tau; vascular amyloid deposition (CAA) commonly coexists.

revised.title: Alzheimer disease neuropathology clues
revised.explanation: Alzheimer disease brains show extracellular amyloid-beta plaques, intracellular tau tangles, eosinophilic Hirano bodies in the hippocampus, and frequent amyloid deposition in vessel walls.

Look-alike inclusions include Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein) and Pick bodies (tau in frontotemporal dementia).

Intracellular aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau form neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons. Their number correlates with the degree of dementia.
Hirano bodies are eosinophilic, rod-shaped intracellular inclusions rich in actin, found in hippocampal neurons and associated with Alzheimer disease.
Amyloid-beta deposits in the walls of cortical and meningeal vessels in most Alzheimer brains, weakening them and predisposing to lobar intracerebral hemorrhage.

original.explanation: These are potentially treatable conditions that can contribute to or mimic a dementia presentation and should be screened for in cognitive decline.

revised.title: Potentially treatable contributors to cognitive impairment
revised.explanation: Each is a treatable condition that can cause or mimic cognitive decline and is screened for when evaluating dementia.

Neurodegenerative dementias such as Alzheimer disease are the contrast group.

Thyroid hormone deficiency slows cognition and causes memory problems that can improve with levothyroxine replacement.
Tertiary syphilis can cause a progressive dementia (general paresis). Penicillin can halt progression, although established deficits may persist.
Cobalamin deficiency can cause cognitive impairment along with subacute combined degeneration and megaloblastic anemia, and it is treatable with B12 replacement.

Myoclonic seizures are brief, shock-like muscle jerks, as in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, typically without loss of awareness.
Atonic seizures cause sudden loss of postural tone, producing head drops or falls (drop attacks).

original.title: Classic narcolepsy symptom tetrad
original.explanation: Narcolepsy can combine excessive daytime sleepiness with REM-intrusion phenomena: cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations.

revised.title: Classic narcolepsy symptom tetrad
revised.explanation: Narcolepsy combines excessive daytime sleepiness with intrusion of REM sleep phenomena into wakefulness: cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hallucinations at sleep onset or awakening.

PSY-007.detail: Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) neurons, which normally stabilize wakefulness and suppress REM sleep. Sleep paralysis is a brief inability to move while falling asleep or waking up, caused by persistent REM atonia.
Vivid dream-like hallucinations occur at sleep onset (hypnagogic) or on awakening (hypnopompic), reflecting REM dream activity intruding into wakefulness.

original.explanation: Prolonged undernutrition in anorexia can produce fine lanugo hair, reproductive suppression (amenorrhea), reduced bone density, and nutrient deficits; these are complications, not mandatory criteria.

revised.title: Clinical clues to anorexia-related undernutrition

Low leptin and suppressed GnRH cause hypothalamic amenorrhea and low estrogen, which, together with low body weight and high cortisol, leads to bone loss. revised.title: SSRIs inhibiting serotonin reuptake
revised.explanation: These selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors block the presynaptic serotonin transporter, raising synaptic serotonin.

revised.title: Lithium-associated adverse effects
revised.explanation: Long-term lithium impairs renal water reabsorption, thyroid hormone release and parathyroid calcium sensing, and commonly causes a fine tremor.

Fine tremor is common at therapeutic levels, while coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion suggest toxicity. Ebstein anomaly is a separate prenatal exposure association.

original.title: Classic neuroleptic malignant syndrome findings
original.explanation: NMS classically combines hyperthermia, marked (lead-pipe) rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability after dopamine blockade.

revised.explanation: After dopamine D2 blockade, neuroleptic malignant syndrome produces severe lead-pipe rigidity with muscle breakdown (high CK), altered mental status and autonomic instability.

Its features are hyperthermia, generalized rigidity, altered mental status and autonomic instability, with markedly elevated CK and possible myoglobinuric renal failure. Confusion, agitation or reduced consciousness progressing to stupor is a core feature.
Labile blood pressure, tachycardia, tachypnea and diaphoresis reflect autonomic dysregulation.

original.title: Mesonephric duct derivatives
original.explanation: The male internal reproductive ducts develop from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct under testosterone stimulation.

revised.title: Mesonephric duct derivatives
revised.explanation: Each structure develops from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct: in males under testosterone stimulation, and in females as a vestigial remnant when the duct regresses.

The paramesonephric (Mullerian) duct is the contrast: it forms the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and upper vagina in females and leaves the appendix testis in males.

Gartner duct is the vestigial mesonephric duct remnant in females, lying along the lateral wall of the vagina or uterus, where it can form a Gartner duct cyst.
The seminal vesicle buds from the distal mesonephric duct and produces most of the seminal fluid, including fructose.
The ejaculatory duct forms from the terminal mesonephric duct beyond the seminal vesicle and opens into the prostatic urethra.

original.title: Risk factors for placental abruption
original.explanation: Vasoconstriction/vascular injury (cocaine OR ~4; smoking OR ~1.8-1.9), hypertensive disease (preeclampsia AOR ~2), and uterine leiomyomas (especially large or retroplacental; adjusted RR ~1.9) increase the risk of premature placental separation.

revised.title: Risk factors for placental abruption
revised.explanation: Each increases the risk of premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall, through vasoconstriction and vascular injury, hypertensive placental vasculopathy, or shearing force.

REPRO-013.detail: Placental abruption presents with painful vaginal bleeding, a tender, firm uterus and possible fetal distress or DIC. Risk factors include hypertension and preeclampsia, cocaine, smoking, abdominal trauma (such as motor vehicle collision or assault), prior abruption and rapid uterine decompression. Placenta previa is the contrast: typically painless bleeding from a placenta covering the cervical os, with risk factors of prior cesarean delivery and multiparity.

Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy damage decidual spiral arteries, predisposing to abruption.
Blunt abdominal trauma, such as a motor vehicle collision, can shear the inelastic placenta from the elastic uterine wall.

original.title: States of prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure
original.explanation: Each produces estrogen stimulation of the endometrium without adequate progesterone opposition (anovulation in PCOS, exogenous estrogen without a progestogen, prolonged endogenous exposure with late menopause, and estrogen-secreting tumors such as granulosa cell tumor), promoting endometrial proliferation, hyperplasia, and type I endometrial carcinoma.

revised.title: States of prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure
revised.explanation: Each exposes the endometrium to estrogen over a long period without adequate progesterone opposition, promoting endometrial hyperplasia and type I endometrial carcinoma.

REPRO-015.detail: Progesterone, produced after ovulation, opposes estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation. Anovulation (PCOS), excess peripheral estrogen production (obesity), a longer reproductive span (late menopause) and estrogen-secreting tumors (granulosa cell tumor) all allow prolonged estrogen stimulation. This explains their shared association with endometrial hyperplasia and endometrioid (type I) endometrial carcinoma. Type II (serous) endometrial carcinoma is not estrogen-driven and arises in atrophic endometrium.

Adipose tissue aromatase converts androgens to estrone, and obesity is often accompanied by anovulation, increasing unopposed estrogen.
A later menopause extends the years of endogenous estrogen exposure, including anovulatory perimenopausal cycles without progesterone.
Granulosa cell tumors of the ovary secrete estrogen, which can cause endometrial hyperplasia, abnormal bleeding or precocious puberty.

original.title: Classic clues to testicular torsion
tiles: Reduced or absent Doppler blood flow
original.explanation: Spermatic cord twisting (often a bell-clapper deformity) produces sudden severe pain, a high-riding/transverse testis, an absent cremasteric reflex, and reduced or absent intratesticular flow on color Doppler (sensitivity ~90-100%).

revised.title: Classic clues to testicular torsion
revised.explanation: Twisting of the spermatic cord, often with a bell-clapper deformity, causes sudden severe scrotal pain, a high-riding testis, loss of the cremasteric reflex and reduced or absent blood flow on color Doppler.

REPRO-024.detail: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency, most common in adolescents, in which rotation of the spermatic cord obstructs venous outflow and then arterial inflow. Testicular salvage is highest with detorsion within about 6 hours. The bell-clapper deformity, inadequate fixation of the testis to the tunica vaginalis, allows the testis to rotate and lie horizontally. Epididymitis is the main look-alike: onset is more gradual, the cremasteric reflex is usually preserved, pain may ease with elevation (Prehn sign), and Doppler flow is increased. Clinical suspicion should not be delayed for imaging, and partial torsion can show some flow.
tileNotes: Abrupt onset of severe unilateral scrotal pain, often with nausea and vomiting, reflects acute ischemia from cord twisting.
Shortening of the twisted cord pulls the testis up, and it often lies horizontally because of a bell-clapper deformity.
Stroking the inner thigh normally elevates the testis. The reflex is usually absent on the affected side in torsion.
Color Doppler ultrasound shows decreased or absent intratesticular blood flow. Normal flow does not exclude partial or intermittent torsion.

original.explanation: These agents can cause drug-induced pulmonary injury that may progress to fibrosis; frequency, mechanism, and predominant pattern differ by drug.

revised.explanation: Each drug can cause drug-induced lung injury that progresses to pulmonary fibrosis.

original.title: Factors shifting the oxygen dissociation curve right
original.explanation: Each reduces hemoglobin oxygen affinity and promotes oxygen unloading at a given oxygen tension.

revised.title: Factors shifting the oxygen dissociation curve right
revised.explanation: Each lowers hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, raising the P50 and promoting oxygen unloading to tissues at a given oxygen tension.

PULM-008.detail: A right shift helps deliver oxygen to metabolically active tissue, which is acidic, warm and rich in CO2. Hydrogen ions and CO2 stabilize the deoxygenated (T) form of hemoglobin (the Bohr effect), heat reduces oxygen binding, and 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin and reduces its affinity; 2,3-BPG rises with chronic hypoxia, high altitude and anemia. The left-shift factors are the mirror image (alkalemia, hypothermia, hypocapnia, low 2,3-BPG), plus fetal hemoglobin and carbon monoxide.

A higher temperature, as in exercising muscle or fever, weakens the hemoglobin-oxygen bond and favors unloading.
Increased CO2 lowers pH and forms carbamino compounds with hemoglobin, both reducing oxygen affinity.
2,3-bisphosphoglycerate binds deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the T state. Levels rise in chronic hypoxia, high altitude and anemia.

original.title: Intrathoracic manifestations of asbestos exposure
original.explanation: Asbestos can cause benign pleural disease (calcified plaques, benign effusion), malignant pleural mesothelioma, and parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis).

revised.title: Consequences of asbestos exposure
revised.explanation: Each is an established disease or finding caused by inhaled asbestos fibers, spanning benign pleural disease, two malignancies, and parenchymal fibrosis.

PULM-017.detail: Asbestos fibers cause benign pleural changes (calcified plaques), malignant mesothelioma, bronchogenic carcinoma, and asbestosis, a fibrosis that favors the lower lobes. Bronchogenic carcinoma is the most common malignancy in exposed patients, and the risk multiplies with smoking. Mesothelioma is the most specific asbestos malignancy but is less common than lung carcinoma. Unlike silicosis and coal workers' pneumoconiosis, which favor the upper lobes, asbestosis is a lower-lobe process.
tileNotes: Calcified plaques on the parietal pleura and diaphragm are the most common sign of prior asbestos exposure and are benign.
A malignancy of mesothelial cells, usually pleural, strongly associated with asbestos even without smoking; psammoma bodies may be seen.
Lung carcinoma is the most common cancer in asbestos-exposed patients, and asbestos and smoking act synergistically.
Asbestosis is a diffuse interstitial fibrosis that predominantly affects the lower lobes, with ferruginous (asbestos) bodies in tissue.
